p: Welcome to the Explorers' Club! We are happy to have you with us. Before your first mission, please read these rules carefully. They have been written to keep everyone safe.

First, you must always carry your club card. If you lose it, tell the front desk immediately. Second, you mustn't enter a portal alone. Even experienced explorers work in pairs. Third, you should check the weather before every mission, because storms can make portals unstable.

New members don't have to buy their own equipment. The club lends helmets, maps and radios for free. However, you have to return them within three days. If you damage something, you might have to pay for it.
Finally, remember that asking for help is not a weakness. Our trainers have helped hundreds of explorers since the club opened in 2010. Good luck, and enjoy the climb!

p: Many adults believe that they are simply too old to learn a new language. Although it is true that children tend to acquire accents more easily, research suggests that adults have important advantages of their own.

Adults usually understand grammar faster, since they can compare it with their first language. Moreover, they are often more motivated, because they learn for a clear reason, such as work or travel. What they tend to lack is not ability, but time and consistency.

Studies indicate that short daily sessions are far more effective than long, occasional ones. In other words, ten minutes a day may well be better than two hours on a Sunday. Not only does regular practice strengthen memory, but it also reduces the anxiety that many learners feel.
Therefore, the question is not whether adults can learn, but how they can build a habit that fits their lives. As one teacher put it, fluency is not a talent. It's a routine.

t: O Homem que Plantou uma Floresta
p: In 1979, a teenager named Jadav Payeng found hundreds of dead snakes on a sandbank in the Brahmaputra River in northeast India. A flood had left them there, and there were no trees to give them shade, so they had died in the heat.

Jadav was shocked. He asked the local forestry department for help, but they told him nothing would grow on the sandbank. So he decided to do it himself. He planted bamboo first, because it grows quickly, and carried water to the young plants every day.

Year after year, he kept planting. He brought red ants from his village to improve the soil, and slowly other trees began to grow. Birds arrived, then deer, rhinos and even tigers. Decades later, his forest covers more than five hundred hectares, an area larger than New York's Central Park.

For a long time, almost nobody knew about it. Officials only discovered the forest in 2008, when they followed a group of elephants into it. Since then, Jadav has received national awards, and the forest is known by his nickname: Molai.

When journalists ask him why he did it, his answer is simple. He says that nature gives us everything, and that each person can give something back. He still lives near the forest with his family and keeps planting trees today.

t: Guia: Seu Primeiro Mês num Emprego Novo
p: Starting a new job is exciting, but the first month can also be stressful. You have to learn new systems, remember dozens of names and show what you can do, all at the same time. Here are five tips to help you settle in.

1. Listen more than you speak. In the first few weeks, your main goal is to understand how things work. Ask questions, take notes and notice how decisions are made. People will respect you more if you understand the situation before you suggest changes.

2. Learn names quickly. Write down the names of the people you meet and what they do. Using someone's name the second time you meet them makes a great impression, and it will help you know who to ask when you have a problem.

3. Ask for feedback early. Don't wait for your first official review. After two or three weeks, ask your manager a simple question: “Is there anything I should be doing differently?” It shows that you care, and it helps you fix small problems before they become big ones.

4. Don't say yes to everything. New employees often accept every task to look helpful, and then they can't finish anything well. It's fine to say, “I'd be happy to help, but I'm working on the report. Which one is more urgent?”

5. Be kind to yourself. Everybody makes mistakes at the beginning. What matters is how you deal with them. Admit the mistake, fix it if you can, and learn from it. In a few months, you'll be the one helping the new person.

p: Twenty years ago, night trains in Europe seemed to be disappearing. Cheap flights had made them look slow and old-fashioned, and many routes were closed. Today, however, they are making a surprising comeback.

New routes now connect cities such as Paris, Vienna, Berlin, Amsterdam and Prague. Passengers can board in the evening, sleep in a bed and wake up in the centre of another city, without the long queues and security checks of an airport.

One reason for their return is the climate. A journey by train produces much less carbon than the same trip by plane, and many travellers, especially younger ones, want to reduce their impact. Some governments have also invested money in new carriages and routes.

But night trains are not perfect. Tickets can be more expensive than a budget flight, especially if you want a private cabin. Trains are sometimes delayed, and sleeping is not always easy when the carriage moves and other passengers snore.

Still, for many people, the experience is part of the holiday. “On a plane, you just want to arrive,” says one regular traveller. “On a night train, the journey itself is an adventure. You fall asleep in one country and have breakfast in another.”

t: Por que os Adolescentes Dormem Tarde
p: Parents often complain that their teenage children stay up until midnight and are impossible to wake in the morning. It is tempting to blame phones, or simple laziness. However, scientists have found that something deeper is going on.

During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts. The hormone melatonin, which makes us feel sleepy, is released about two hours later than in children or adults. As a result, a typical teenager is not biologically ready to sleep until around eleven at night, and naturally wants to wake up around eight.

The problem is that most schools start early. A student who falls asleep at eleven and has to get up at half past six will regularly get far less than the eight to ten hours that teenagers need. Over time, this sleep debt can affect mood, concentration, memory and even physical health.

Some schools have experimented with later start times, and the results have been encouraging. Studies in several countries have reported better attendance, fewer students falling asleep in class, and in some cases improved grades. Car accidents involving young drivers also fell in one region after schools changed their timetable.

Not everyone is convinced. Moving the school day affects buses, parents' working hours and after-school activities, and critics argue that teenagers would simply go to bed even later. Yet the evidence suggests that, at least to some extent, teenagers' late nights are not a choice. Expecting them to be alert at eight in the morning may be like expecting adults to be at their best at five.

t: Carta ao Jornal: Salvem a Biblioteca
p: Dear Editor,

I am writing to express my deep concern about the council's plan to close the Riverside Library and replace it with a small digital kiosk in the shopping centre. According to last week's report, the change would save around £80,000 a year. I would argue that the real cost would be much higher.

For many residents, the library is far more than a place to borrow books. It is one of the few warm, free public spaces left in our town. Every morning, I see elderly people reading newspapers, parents at the toddlers' story time, and job seekers using the computers to write their CVs. A kiosk in a shopping centre cannot offer any of this.

The council claims that “people now read online”. While it is true that e-books are popular, a recent national survey found that libraries are used most by those with the least money: exactly the people who may not have a reliable internet connection at home. Closing the library would hit them hardest.

I appreciate that the council is under serious financial pressure, and I am not suggesting that nothing can change. Opening hours could be adjusted, volunteers could help, and the building could be shared with other services, such as a health clinic. Several towns have done exactly this, with great success.
I urge the council to consult residents properly before making a decision that cannot easily be reversed. Once a library is gone, it rarely comes back.
Yours faithfully, Margaret Ellis

p: When Dr Sarah Okafor started using an AI system to analyse X-rays last year, she was sceptical. “I assumed it would either be useless or try to replace me,” she says. Twelve months later, she describes it as “a very fast, very tireless junior colleague who still needs supervision.”

The system she uses has been trained on millions of images and highlights areas that might show a fracture or an early sign of disease. In tests, similar tools have matched or exceeded the accuracy of experienced doctors at certain narrow tasks, such as spotting some types of cancer on scans.

The benefits are clear in busy hospitals. Doctors can check urgent cases first, and fewer small problems are missed at the end of a long shift, when tiredness makes mistakes more likely. In regions with few specialists, such tools could give patients access to a faster diagnosis.

However, the technology has limits. AI systems can perform worse on groups of patients who were under-represented in the data they learned from, and they rarely explain why they reached a conclusion. “If it flags something, I still have to understand the whole patient,” Dr Okafor says. “It doesn't know that the person in front of me fell off a ladder yesterday.”

There are also difficult questions about responsibility. If an AI tool misses a tumour, who is to blame: the doctor, the hospital or the company that built it? For now, most experts agree that the safest approach is a partnership, in which machines assist and humans decide.

p: There has never been more advice on how to get things done. Productivity apps promise to organise our lives, podcasts reveal the morning routines of billionaires, and an entire industry sells the idea that, with the right system, we could accomplish almost anything. Yet surveys consistently suggest that people feel busier and more exhausted than ever.

Part of the problem, I would argue, lies in what we mean by productivity. The concept was developed for factories, where output could be counted: more cars per hour meant a more productive worker. Applied to knowledge work, or to life in general, the metaphor becomes misleading. Writing a thoughtful report, raising a child or recovering from an illness cannot be meaningfully measured in units per hour.

Moreover, efficiency tends to generate its own demand. When email made communication faster, we did not finish our work sooner; we simply sent more emails. The time saved by one tool is quickly absorbed by new expectations, so that we run faster merely to stay in the same place.

None of this is to dismiss the value of planning or focus. Breaking a large task into smaller steps, or protecting a few hours from interruptions, genuinely helps. The difficulty arises when these techniques become ends in themselves, and when every spare moment is treated as an opportunity to optimise rather than to rest.

Perhaps a more useful question is not “How can I do more?” but “What is actually worth doing?” Answering it requires something that no app can provide: the willingness to accept that our time is finite, that some things will remain undone, and that this is not a personal failure but simply the human condition.

p: In 1777, a woman named Dolly Pentreath died in a small fishing village in Cornwall, in the far south-west of England. She is often described as the last native speaker of Cornish, a Celtic language closely related to Welsh and Breton. For almost two centuries afterwards, Cornish was regarded as dead.

Yet the story is more complicated than a single death. Historians have since found evidence that fragments of the language survived in fishing communities, in counting rhymes and in place names, long after 1777. Languages rarely vanish overnight; they retreat gradually, from public life to the home, and finally to a handful of words that people no longer fully understand.

In the early twentieth century, a small group of enthusiasts began reconstructing Cornish from old manuscripts and dictionaries. Their work was painstaking and, at times, fiercely contested: rival versions of spelling and pronunciation divided the revival movement for decades, until a standard written form was agreed in 2008.

Today, a few hundred people are thought to speak Cornish fluently, and several thousand have some knowledge of it. There are children's books, radio programmes and a small number of families raising their children with Cornish at home. In 2010, UNESCO changed the language's status from “extinct” to “critically endangered”, a rare reclassification.

Sceptics question whether a language learned from books can ever be truly alive. Supporters reply that every revived language, including Hebrew, began in exactly this way. Ultimately, perhaps, a language lives not when it is perfectly preserved, but when people choose to use it in their everyday lives, to argue, to joke and to comfort their children.

p: Purpose. This report summarises the results of the six-month hybrid working pilot, in which staff in three departments worked from the office on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays, and remotely on Mondays and Fridays. It concludes with recommendations for the management board.

Findings. Overall, the pilot was well received. In the final survey, 78% of participants rated the arrangement as positive, citing reduced commuting time and fewer interruptions as the main benefits. Sick leave fell by 14% compared with the same period last year, and staff turnover in the participating departments was the lowest recorded in five years.

However, several concerns emerged. New employees reported feeling less connected to their teams and found it harder to learn informally from more experienced colleagues. Managers noted that collaboration across departments had decreased, as people tended to communicate only with their immediate team on office days. In addition, demand for meeting rooms on Tuesdays and Wednesdays frequently exceeded supply.

Recommendations. First, the hybrid model should be extended to all departments, subject to a review after twelve months. Second, new employees should spend their first six weeks primarily in the office, each paired with an experienced mentor. Third, one office day per month should be designated for cross-department projects and social events. Finally, the booking system for meeting rooms should be upgraded, and at least two small rooms converted into spaces for focused individual work.

Conclusion. The pilot suggests that hybrid working can improve wellbeing and retention without reducing performance, provided that deliberate steps are taken to protect the informal learning and collaboration that tend to happen naturally in a shared workplace.

t: Como os Pombos Voltam para Casa
p: For thousands of years, people have used pigeons to carry messages. Release a homing pigeon hundreds of kilometres from its loft, in a place it has never seen, and it will usually find its way back within a day. Yet scientists still do not fully understand how they do it.

Part of the answer appears to be the sun. Experiments in the 1950s showed that pigeons use the position of the sun as a compass, adjusting for the time of day with their internal clock. When researchers shifted the birds' body clocks by keeping them in artificial light, the pigeons flew off in predictably wrong directions.

But a compass alone is not enough. To get home, you need to know not only which way is north, but also where you are. Pigeons released on cloudy days, when the sun is hidden, still find their way, which suggests that they have other tools as well.

One possibility is the Earth's magnetic field. Some studies have found that strong magnets attached to pigeons confuse them, especially under cloudy skies. Another is smell: pigeons whose sense of smell has been blocked often struggle to navigate from unfamiliar places, which has led some researchers to propose that they build a kind of map from the scents carried by the wind.

There is also evidence that experienced pigeons memorise landmarks. GPS tracking has shown birds following motorways, rivers and railway lines, sometimes even turning at the same junctions as cars. Rather than a single magical sense, it seems likely that pigeons combine several sources of information, relying more on one or another depending on the conditions.

This flexibility is perhaps the most impressive part of the story. Like an experienced traveller who uses a map, road signs and the position of the sun, pigeons seem to use whatever information is available. After more than half a century of research, the humble pigeon remains one of nature's most remarkable navigators.

t: Coluna: Em Defesa do Tédio no Trabalho
p: Every few months, a new study reveals that office workers spend an alarming amount of their day in meetings, answering emails or switching between tasks. The usual response is a fresh round of advice on how to cut meetings and get more done. I would like to suggest something slightly different.

Most of us have experienced a strange phenomenon: our best ideas rarely arrive at our desks. They come in the shower, on a walk, or while doing the washing-up. This is not a coincidence. When the mind is not focused on a specific task, it begins to wander, connecting memories and ideas in unexpected ways.

The modern workplace leaves almost no room for this. Every gap in the day is filled with a notification, a quick message or another meeting. Even our breaks are spent scrolling through our phones. We have become extremely efficient at being busy, and surprisingly bad at thinking.

Some companies have started to experiment. One software firm introduced a rule that Wednesday afternoons are free of meetings and messages. Staff can do what they like, as long as it is not routine work. Many reported that this quiet time produced their most creative work of the week.

I am not suggesting that we should all spend our working hours staring out of the window. Deadlines are real, and some jobs leave very little flexibility. But managers who measure productivity only by visible activity may be missing something important. The employee who appears to be doing nothing might, in fact, be solving the problem that everyone else is too busy to notice.
So the next time you catch yourself gazing into space at work, don't feel guilty. You might be doing the most valuable thing you'll do all day.

t: Guia: Como Ler uma Notícia Científica
p: “Coffee prevents cancer.” “Chocolate helps you lose weight.” Headlines like these appear every week, often contradicting the ones from the week before. How can a non-scientist tell which claims deserve attention? Here are five questions worth asking.

1. Who was studied? Many exciting results come from experiments on mice or cells in a laboratory. These are important first steps, but what works in a mouse frequently fails in humans. If the headline doesn't mention it, check whether the study involved people at all.

2. How many people took part? A study of twenty volunteers can suggest an idea, but it can easily produce a result by chance. Larger studies, involving thousands of participants, are generally more reliable, especially when their findings are repeated by other teams.

3. Does it show cause, or just a link? Suppose researchers find that people who drink more coffee live longer. That does not prove coffee is responsible. Coffee drinkers might also be wealthier, or more active. Only carefully designed experiments, in which people are randomly assigned to different groups, can show that one thing actually causes another.

4. How big is the effect? A headline might say that something “doubles your risk” of a disease. That sounds frightening, but if the original risk was one in a million, doubling it means two in a million: still extremely small. Always look for the actual numbers.

5. Who paid for it? Funding from a company does not automatically make research wrong, but it is worth knowing. A study on the benefits of a drink paid for by the company that sells it deserves a little extra scepticism.
None of these questions requires a science degree. They simply ask you to slow down before sharing a headline, which is, perhaps, the most scientific habit of all.

t: Perfil: A Mulher que Contava Estrelas
p: In the 1890s, the Harvard College Observatory employed a group of women to examine photographs of the night sky. They were paid less than the men who operated the telescopes, and their job was described as “computing”. Among them was Henrietta Swan Leavitt, whose discovery would change our understanding of the size of the universe.

Leavitt was studying a type of star called a Cepheid, whose brightness rises and falls in a regular cycle. Working through thousands of photographic plates, she noticed something remarkable: the brighter the star, the longer its cycle. In 1912, she published this relationship, which became known as Leavitt's law.

Its importance was not immediately obvious, but astronomers soon realised what it meant. If you know how bright a star really is, and you measure how bright it appears from Earth, you can calculate how far away it is. Cepheids became a kind of measuring tape for the universe.

Within a decade, Edwin Hubble used Cepheids to show that some fuzzy patches in the sky were not clouds within our galaxy, but entire galaxies of their own, millions of light years away. The universe, it turned out, was vastly larger than anyone had imagined. Hubble himself acknowledged that Leavitt's work had made his findings possible.

Leavitt did not live to see much of this. She died of cancer in 1921, aged fifty-three. A few years later, a Swedish mathematician wrote to Harvard to say he wished to nominate her for the Nobel Prize, unaware that she had already died. The prize cannot be awarded after death.

Today, her name is attached to a crater on the Moon and an asteroid, and her law remains one of the foundations of modern astronomy. Her story is also a reminder of how many important contributions have been made by people whose work was considered routine.

p: It seems self-evident that more choice is better. If one supermarket offers five kinds of jam and another offers fifty, the second surely serves its customers better: whatever your taste, you are more likely to find exactly what you want. Freedom, after all, is largely the freedom to choose.

Yet a well-known experiment complicated this assumption. Shoppers who were offered a tasting table with twenty-four varieties of jam were more likely to stop and look, but far less likely to buy anything than those offered just six. Faced with an abundance of options, many people simply walked away.

Psychologists have proposed several reasons for this. Comparing many alternatives is mentally exhausting, and the effort can outweigh the pleasure of the eventual choice. Moreover, the more options we reject, the more we are likely to wonder whether one of them would have been better, so that even a good decision can leave us dissatisfied. Abundant choice also raises our expectations: with so much available, surely the perfect option exists, and settling for anything less feels like a failure.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that choice is simply harmful. Later attempts to replicate the jam study produced mixed results, and the effect appears to depend heavily on context. When people know exactly what they want, or when options are clearly organised, a wide selection rarely causes paralysis. For complex decisions such as pensions or medical treatments, however, an overwhelming range of options can lead people to avoid deciding at all, sometimes to their considerable cost.

Perhaps the most practical lesson concerns not how many options exist, but how we approach them. Some researchers distinguish between “maximisers”, who seek the best possible option, and “satisficers”, who are content with one that is good enough. Intriguingly, maximisers often make objectively better choices, yet feel worse about them. In a world that offers almost limitless variety, the ability to decide when something is good enough may be one of the more underrated skills.

q.q: Ideia geral: qual é a tese do ensaio?
o: Mais opções nem sempre trazem mais satisfação, dependendo do contexto.
Os supermercados deveriam vender menos geleias.

q.q: Detalhe: o que aconteceu no experimento das geleias?
o: Com 24 sabores, mais gente parou, mas menos gente comprou.

q.q: Detalhe: qual é uma razão psicológica citada?
o: Comparar muitas opções cansa e aumenta o arrependimento.
As pessoas não gostam de geleia.

q.q: Opinião: o autor conclui que escolha é simplesmente prejudicial?
o: Não: os resultados variam e dependem do contexto.

q.q: Detalhe: qual é a diferença entre maximizers e satisficers?
o: Uns buscam o melhor possível; os outros se contentam com o bom o bastante.
Uns compram mais; os outros, menos.
Uns são ricos; os outros, pobres.

t: Reportagem: A Cidade que Proibiu os Carros no Centro
p: When the Spanish city of Pontevedra banned most cars from its historic centre in 1999, local shopkeepers predicted disaster. Without customers able to park outside their doors, they argued, businesses would collapse and the old town would be left to decay. Two decades later, the reality has turned out rather differently.

The change was introduced by a newly elected mayor who argued that the city belonged to its residents rather than to their vehicles. Streets in the centre were turned over to pedestrians, with access for cars limited to deliveries, emergency services and residents' garages. Underground and free surface car parks were provided on the edges of the zone, within a short walk of the centre.

The effects went well beyond reduced traffic. Air pollution fell substantially, and road deaths in the city dropped dramatically over the following years. Perhaps more strikingly, the population of the centre, which had been declining, began to grow again as families returned to streets that were now quiet and safe enough for children to play in.

The predicted collapse of local businesses did not materialise. Although some shops closed, others opened, attracted by the steady flow of people on foot. Pedestrians, it turns out, tend to linger, browse and return more often than drivers, who visit a single shop and leave.

Critics point out that Pontevedra is a relatively small city, and that what works in a compact historic centre may be much harder to achieve in a sprawling metropolis built around the car. Others note that the transition required years of patient negotiation, and that some residents, particularly elderly people living outside the centre, initially found access more difficult.

Nevertheless, delegations from cities across Europe and beyond have visited to study the model. The lesson they tend to take away is not that cars should be banned everywhere, but that the default assumption, that streets exist primarily for traffic, is a choice rather than a law of nature, and one that can be reversed.

t: Carta Formal: Contestação de uma Multa
p: Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to appeal against the parking penalty notice issued to my vehicle on 3 October at 14:20 on Wilton Road. I believe the penalty was issued in error, for the reasons set out below, and I would respectfully request that it be cancelled.

According to the notice, my car was parked in a restricted bay without a valid permit. However, I had purchased a two-hour ticket through the council's parking app at 13:05, a copy of which I have attached, together with the confirmation email. The ticket was therefore valid until 15:05, well beyond the time at which the penalty was issued.

I appreciate that the civil enforcement officer may not have been able to see the electronic ticket, as the app does not always update the council's system immediately. I understand that this is a known issue, as several residents have reported similar problems on the local community forum in recent weeks. I would suggest that this may warrant further investigation, so that other drivers are not penalised unfairly.

I have also attached two photographs, taken when I returned to my vehicle, showing the signs in the bay. These indicate that the bay is available to permit holders and to drivers with a valid ticket, which is consistent with my understanding of the rules.

In light of the above, I trust that you will agree that the penalty should not stand. I would be grateful if you could confirm the cancellation in writing at your earliest convenience. Should you require any further information, please do not hesitate to contact me.
Yours faithfully, Beatriz Souza

t: Artigo: Por que Ainda Escrevemos à Mão
p: In many classrooms, the pen is quietly giving way to the keyboard. Students take notes on laptops, submit essays online and, increasingly, sit exams on screens. Typing is faster, easier to edit and, for many, more legible than their handwriting. So why do some researchers argue that handwriting still deserves a place in education?

One widely cited study compared students who took lecture notes by hand with those who used laptops. Those typing wrote considerably more, often recording the lecture almost word for word. Yet when tested on the material, the handwriting group tended to perform better on conceptual questions. The researchers suggested that because writing by hand is slower, it forces students to summarise and rephrase, processing the ideas rather than transcribing them.

Subsequent attempts to replicate this finding have produced mixed results, and the advantage may be smaller than first reported. Nevertheless, the underlying principle, that deeper processing leads to better learning, is well supported. A laptop user who deliberately summarises rather than transcribes may gain much of the same benefit.

For young children, the case for handwriting appears stronger. Forming letters by hand seems to help children recognise them, and some brain-imaging studies have found greater activity in reading-related areas after children practised writing letters compared with typing them. Handwriting, in this view, is not merely a way of recording language but part of the process of learning it.

None of this amounts to an argument against technology. Typing is an essential skill, and for students with certain learning difficulties, keyboards and speech-to-text tools can be genuinely liberating. The more nuanced conclusion is that tools shape thinking in different ways, and that the most effective choice depends on the task. Taking notes in a lecture, drafting a novel and filling in a form are different activities, and there is no reason to assume a single tool suits them all.

p: Do you know why a sandwich is called a sandwich? The story begins in England in the 18th century.

John Montagu was the fourth Earl of Sandwich, a town in the south-east of England. According to the story, he loved playing cards and didn't want to stop for meals. So he asked for some meat between two pieces of bread. That way, he could eat with one hand and keep playing with the other.

His friends started to ask for “the same as Sandwich”, and the name stayed. Some historians say he actually ate this way because he was busy working, not playing cards. We will probably never know the truth.
Of course, people ate bread with food inside long before the Earl was born. But today, thanks to him, millions of people around the world eat a “sandwich” every day.
